description: Held-out evaluation prompts for Explanation Lab V0. Topics deliberately avoid the research archive's topics (caching, B-tree indexes, TCP handshake, vaccines, compound interest) and every topic used in the skill's own examples. Send 'question' exactly as written. For follow-up cases, send 'context' and 'question' together as one message, in the format given in RUNBOOK.md.

fields.skill_expectation: should_apply: an explanation request where the skill's operations are relevant. apply_briefly: explanation is secondary or a short answer is requested. should_not_apply: no teaching should be added.
fields.expected_length: one_sentence | short (under ~120 words) | medium (~120-450 words) | long_ok (depth requested or intrinsically multi-step). Guidance for the appropriate-depth rating, not a hard rule.

cases.question: What is DNA actually doing inside a cell? People call it a 'code', but I don't understand what it's a code for.
cases.audience: Adult with no biology since secondary school
expected_properties: Explains that DNA stores instructions mainly for building proteins (and functional RNAs)
Connects gene to RNA to protein in order (transcription, then translation)
Explains why 'code' fits: sequences of three bases specify amino acids
Says what proteins do, so the reader knows why the instructions matter
common_misconceptions: DNA itself performs the cell's work
All DNA codes for proteins
Each gene is a single trait

critical_facts.fact: Genes are DNA segments that are transcribed into RNA
Messenger RNA is translated by ribosomes into a chain of amino acids (a protein)
A codon of three nucleotides specifies one amino acid or a stop signal
Much of the genome does not code for proteins

reasoning_gaps: Jumping from 'DNA' to 'proteins' without the RNA intermediate
Using 'gene expression' or 'codon' without introducing them

cases.question: What is inflation, and why would printing more money cause it?
cases.audience: General adult reader with no economics training
expected_properties: Defines inflation as a sustained rise in the general price level, or a fall in what money buys
Explains the mechanism linking more money to higher prices (more money chasing the same goods)
Preserves the nuance that the link is not automatic or proportional
Mentions that inflation has other causes
common_misconceptions: Printing money always raises prices immediately and proportionally
Inflation means every price rises by the same amount
A single price rising is inflation

critical_facts.fact: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in prices across the economy
Money growth that outpaces the economy's output of goods and services tends to push prices up
The relationship depends on conditions such as spare capacity and how much new money is spent; it is not mechanical
Inflation can also come from other sources, such as supply shocks or rising demand

reasoning_gaps: Asserting 'more money means higher prices' without saying why
Dropping the hedge and presenting the relationship as a law

cases.question: What does a compiler do, and why can't a computer just run my C code directly?
cases.audience: Someone who has written a little code but never studied how computers execute it
expected_properties: Establishes first that a processor executes only its own machine instructions
Explains that the compiler translates C into machine code ahead of time
Explains why the translation is needed (C is written for humans; the CPU decodes binary instructions)
Optionally contrasts with interpreters without derailing
common_misconceptions: The CPU understands C or other programming languages
Compiling just makes the same text run faster
A compiled program runs on any processor type

critical_facts.fact: A CPU executes machine instructions defined by its instruction set architecture
A compiler translates source code into machine code (often through intermediate steps) before the program runs
Machine code is specific to a processor architecture (and usually an operating system)

reasoning_gaps: Saying 'translates to machine code' without saying why the CPU needs that
Introducing assembly, linking, or object files without need

cases.question: What is voltage? Every explanation says 'potential difference' and I don't know what that means.
cases.audience: Adult learner who knows that electricity involves moving charge, but no physics vocabulary
expected_properties: Builds 'potential difference' from energy and charge rather than repeating the phrase
Explains that voltage is always between two points
Connects voltage to why current flows when there is a path
Any analogy (e.g. water pressure or height) states where it breaks
common_misconceptions: Voltage flows through a circuit
Voltage and current are the same thing
A single point has a voltage with no reference point

critical_facts.fact: Voltage is the difference in electric potential energy per unit charge between two points (one volt is one joule per coulomb)
Current flows when a conducting path connects points at different potentials
Voltage is defined between two points; 'the voltage at a point' implies a reference point such as ground

reasoning_gaps: Using 'potential' or 'electric potential energy' without building it
Analogy presented as the full truth

cases.question: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon when they've both been sitting in the same room?
expected_properties: States that both spoons are at the same temperature
Explains that metal conducts heat away from the skin much faster than wood
Explains that the sensation of cold reflects heat leaving the skin, not the object's temperature
common_misconceptions: The metal spoon is actually colder
Metal contains or emits 'cold'

critical_facts.fact: Objects left in the same room reach the same temperature
Metal has much higher thermal conductivity than wood, so it draws heat from warmer skin faster
Touch senses the rate of heat loss and skin cooling, not the object's temperature directly

reasoning_gaps: Saying 'metal conducts heat better' without linking that to the sensation
Omitting that the temperatures are equal

cases.question: How do antibiotics kill bacteria without killing our own cells?
cases.audience: Nursing student who knows basic cell biology
expected_properties: Explains selective toxicity: antibiotics target structures or processes that differ between bacteria and human cells
Gives at least one concrete target, such as the bacterial cell wall or bacterial ribosome, with how disruption harms the bacterium
Preserves that selectivity is not perfect (side effects, effects on beneficial bacteria)
Avoids implying antibiotics work on viruses
common_misconceptions: Antibiotics kill viruses
Antibiotics have no effect on human cells or the microbiome
Bacteria become resistant because they 'get used to' the drug, rather than resistant variants being selected

critical_facts.fact: Many antibiotics target features bacteria have and human cells lack or have in a different form, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall or bacterial 70S ribosomes
Beta-lactams such as penicillin interfere with building the peptidoglycan cell wall
Antibiotics do not treat viral infections
Selectivity is not absolute; antibiotics can cause side effects and harm beneficial bacteria

reasoning_gaps: Asserting 'they target bacteria' without saying what differs
Naming drug classes without the mechanism

cases.question: Why does my program sometimes give the wrong total when two threads increment the same counter variable?
cases.audience: Developer comfortable with single-threaded code, new to concurrency
expected_properties: Explains that 'counter += 1' is a read-modify-write sequence, not one indivisible step
Walks through an interleaving where one update is lost
Explains why it is intermittent (depends on timing)
Names a fix (lock or atomic operation) and why it works
common_misconceptions: It can only happen on multi-core machines
Adding print statements or sleeps fixes it
The problem is the variable's data type

critical_facts.fact: Incrementing a shared variable usually involves separate read, add, and write steps
If two threads interleave those steps, one increment can overwrite the other and be lost
A mutex or an atomic increment makes the update indivisible with respect to other threads
The outcome depends on scheduling, so the bug appears intermittently

reasoning_gaps: Saying 'race condition' without showing the interleaving
Recommending a lock without explaining what it prevents

cases.question: Why does spreading salt on an icy road make the ice melt?
expected_properties: Explains that salt dissolves into the thin film of liquid water on the ice
Explains freezing-point depression: the salt solution freezes at a lower temperature than pure water
Mentions the temperature limit below which salt stops working
Does not claim the salt generates heat
common_misconceptions: Salt reacts chemically with ice and releases heat
Salt works at any temperature

critical_facts.fact: Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water (freezing-point depression)
Salt needs some liquid water to dissolve into; ice surfaces usually have a thin liquid layer
Sodium chloride stops being effective at low temperatures (theoretical limit about -21 C; practically less effective below roughly -10 C)

reasoning_gaps: 'Salt lowers the melting point' with no account of why that melts existing ice
Omitting the temperature limit

cases.question: Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise?
cases.audience: Someone who knows what a bond is (a loan that pays fixed interest) but not how bonds are priced
expected_properties: Starts from the fact that an existing bond's coupon payments are fixed
Explains that when new bonds pay more, buyers will only buy the old bond at a lower price
Shows (ideally with illustrative numbers) that the lower price raises the old bond's effective yield to market levels
Optionally notes longer-maturity bonds are more sensitive
common_misconceptions: The bond's coupon rate changes when market rates change
Holding a bond to maturity means losing the principal after a price drop (absent default)

critical_facts.fact: A fixed-rate bond's coupon payments do not change after issue
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions
Absent default, a bond held to maturity still repays its face value
Longer-maturity bonds are generally more sensitive to rate changes

reasoning_gaps: Stating the inverse relationship without the 'competing with new bonds' step
Using 'yield' or 'duration' without introducing them

cases.question: How can one infinity be bigger than another? What does 'uncountably infinite' actually mean?
cases.audience: Adult comfortable with school algebra, no university maths
expected_properties: Introduces comparing sizes by one-to-one pairing before applying it to infinite sets
Defines countable as pairable with the natural numbers
Gives an intuitive version of Cantor's diagonal argument for the real numbers
Avoids treating infinity as an ordinary number
common_misconceptions: Infinity is a single number
The rational numbers are uncountable because they are dense
A set with 'more' elements in the everyday sense (like all integers vs even integers) is larger

critical_facts.fact: Two sets have the same size (cardinality) if their elements can be paired one-to-one
A set is countably infinite if it can be paired one-to-one with the natural numbers
The real numbers cannot be listed in such a pairing (Cantor's diagonal argument), so they are uncountable
The even numbers and the rational numbers are both countable

reasoning_gaps: Stating 'the reals are uncountable' without the pairing idea
Presenting the diagonal argument without saying what it contradicts

cases.question: What does a p-value actually tell me? I keep seeing p < 0.05 in papers.
cases.audience: Graduate student in a non-quantitative field reading research papers
expected_properties: Introduces the null hypothesis before the p-value
Defines the p-value as a probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null (and the model) is true
Explicitly separates it from the probability that the null hypothesis is true
Notes that 0.05 is a convention and that p does not measure effect size or importance
common_misconceptions: p is the probability the null hypothesis is true
p < 0.05 means the result is important or large
p > 0.05 proves there is no effect

critical_facts.fact: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and model assumptions hold, of results at least as extreme as those observed
A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true
The 0.05 threshold is a convention, not a natural boundary
A small p-value does not indicate a large or important effect

reasoning_gaps: Using 'null hypothesis' without introducing it
Defining p correctly then interpreting it incorrectly

cases.question: What is recursion, really? I can follow examples, but I don't see why a function that calls itself doesn't just loop forever.
cases.audience: Beginner programmer who understands functions and if-statements
expected_properties: Explains the base case and that each call works on a smaller or simpler input
Explains that each call has its own variables (its own frame on the call stack) and returns to its caller
Traces a small example to show the calls stopping and unwinding
States what happens without a base case (stack overflow or a recursion limit)
common_misconceptions: Recursive calls share the same variables
Recursion is just a loop with different syntax
The function restarts from the top and forgets where it was

critical_facts.fact: A recursive function needs a base case that returns without recursing
Each recursive call must move toward the base case
Each call has its own local variables and resumes the caller when it returns
Without a reachable base case, calls accumulate until the stack overflows or a recursion limit is hit

reasoning_gaps: Mentioning the base case without explaining why calls reach it
Not explaining how results flow back up

cases.question: What actually happens, step by step, between me tapping my card at a shop and the payment being approved?
expected_properties: Orders the participants (card, terminal, merchant's acquirer or processor, card network, issuing bank) before or as the steps use them
Explains that the issuer decides (funds or credit available, fraud checks)
Distinguishes authorization (seconds) from settlement (later)
Explains why the card produces a one-time code rather than sending static data
common_misconceptions: Money moves to the merchant at the moment of the tap
The shop decides whether the payment is approved
The merchant receives the full card details in a reusable form

critical_facts.fact: The authorization request typically travels from the terminal through the merchant's acquirer or processor and the card network to the issuing bank
The issuing bank approves or declines the authorization
Settlement, the actual transfer of funds, typically happens later than authorization
Chip and contactless cards generate a transaction-specific cryptogram, which makes copied data harder to reuse

reasoning_gaps: Listing parties without saying what each one does
Conflating approval with payment

cases.question: How does a nerve signal travel along a neuron?
expected_properties: Establishes the resting potential before the action potential
Orders the steps: depolarization via sodium channels, repolarization via potassium channels
Explains propagation: each depolarized patch triggers the next
Explains myelin's effect (saltatory conduction) and the all-or-none property
common_misconceptions: Electrons flow down the axon like current in a wire
A stronger stimulus makes a bigger action potential
The signal can travel backwards along the axon as easily

critical_facts.fact: At rest the inside of the neuron is negative relative to the outside
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, sodium enters, and the membrane depolarizes
Potassium leaving the cell repolarizes the membrane
Action potentials are all-or-none; stimulus strength is encoded mainly by firing frequency
In myelinated axons the signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), which speeds it up

reasoning_gaps: Introducing 'depolarization' before the resting potential
Saying the signal 'travels' without explaining propagation

cases.question: How does git actually combine two branches when I run git merge?
cases.audience: Developer who uses git daily for commits and branches but treats merges as magic
expected_properties: Introduces the merge base (common ancestor) before the three-way comparison
Explains that each side's changes are computed relative to the base
Explains when changes combine automatically and when a conflict occurs
Mentions the fast-forward case and the merge commit with two parents
common_misconceptions: Git compares only the two branch tips
A conflict means one branch is broken
Git merges by commit timestamps

critical_facts.fact: Git finds a merge base, a common ancestor commit of the two branches
A three-way merge compares each branch's version against the merge base
Changes to different parts combine automatically; overlapping changes to the same lines produce a conflict
If the current branch has no new commits, git can fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit

reasoning_gaps: Explaining conflicts without the merge base
Using 'three-way merge' as a label without saying what the three versions are

cases.question: What's the difference between a process and a thread, and when would I use each?
cases.audience: Developer who has written single-threaded programs
expected_properties: Identifies memory sharing as the central difference
Derives the tradeoffs from it: cheap communication versus isolation, and synchronization needs
Gives decision guidance tied to those tradeoffs
common_misconceptions: Threads always make a program faster
Processes cannot communicate
Threads in a process have separate memory

critical_facts.fact: Each process has its own address space; threads of one process share it
Threads are generally cheaper to create and switch than processes
Shared memory between threads requires synchronization to avoid data races
Process isolation means one process crashing usually does not corrupt another

reasoning_gaps: A feature table without the shared-memory cause
Advice not linked to the tradeoffs

cases.question: What's the difference between AC and DC electricity, and why does the power grid use AC?
expected_properties: Defines both in terms of current direction
Explains that transformers change AC voltage easily
Explains why high voltage reduces transmission losses for the same power
Preserves the nuance that DC is also used, e.g. high-voltage DC links
common_misconceptions: AC was chosen because it is safer
DC cannot be transmitted over long distances at all

critical_facts.fact: DC flows in one direction; AC reverses direction periodically (50 or 60 times a second on most grids)
Transformers can raise or lower AC voltage efficiently
For the same power, higher voltage means lower current and therefore lower resistive losses in the wires
High-voltage DC is used for some long-distance and undersea links

reasoning_gaps: 'AC is easier to transmit' without the transformer and loss chain
Mentioning I-squared-R without explaining it to a general reader

cases.question: People say correlation isn't causation. How can two things be correlated if one doesn't cause the other?
cases.audience: General adult who reads news about health studies
expected_properties: Explains at least confounding and reverse causation with concrete cases
Mentions chance or selection effects
Explains why randomized experiments help
Avoids implying correlation is worthless as evidence
common_misconceptions: Correlation is never evidence of causation
A strong correlation proves causation

critical_facts.fact: A third factor (a confounder) can cause both variables
The causal direction can run the opposite way from the one assumed
Randomly assigning a treatment balances confounders on average, which supports causal conclusions
Correlation can still be evidence that warrants causal investigation

reasoning_gaps: Naming 'confounding' without an example
Not saying how causation is established instead

cases.question: What's the difference between lossless and lossy compression, and why can lossy files be so much smaller?
cases.audience: Tech-savvy user who edits photos and audio
expected_properties: Explains that lossless compression exploits redundancy and reconstructs the original exactly
Explains that lossy compression discards information judged least noticeable
Explains why discarding information allows much smaller files (there is a limit to lossless compression)
Mentions a consequence such as generational loss from repeated re-encoding
common_misconceptions: Lossless compression can shrink any file
Lossy compression removes data at random
Converting a lossy file to a lossless format restores quality

critical_facts.fact: Lossless compression lets the original data be reconstructed exactly
Lossless compression works by removing redundancy and cannot shrink every possible input
Lossy compression discards information, typically chosen using models of human perception
Discarded information cannot be recovered by converting to a lossless format

reasoning_gaps: Saying lossy 'removes data' without why it can remove more
Format lists (PNG, JPEG, MP3) without the mechanism

cases.question: I get that multiplying by -1 flips a number to the other side of zero, but why does flipping twice give a positive? It still feels like a rule I'm supposed to just memorize.
cases.context: Earlier you explained: "Multiplying by -1 flips a number to the opposite side of zero on the number line, so -1 times 3 is -3."
expected_properties: Addresses only the 'flip twice' link without repeating the whole earlier explanation
Gives a reason rather than restating the rule (for example, two flips return to the start; or a distributive-law argument)
Ties the answer back to the number-line picture the user already has
common_misconceptions: The sign rule is an arbitrary convention
Negative numbers 'cancel' because two minus signs make a plus sign visually

critical_facts.fact: The rule follows from requiring multiplication to distribute over addition (e.g. -1 x (1 + -1) = 0)

reasoning_gaps: Restating the rule as the reason
Repeating the entire first explanation

cases.question: But if a satellite is falling, why doesn't it eventually hit the ground? Doesn't gravity win in the end?
cases.context: Earlier you explained: "Satellites stay in orbit because they are falling around the Earth. They move sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath them as they fall."
expected_properties: Targets the specific gap: at orbital speed the fall matches the Earth's curvature, so the distance to the ground does not shrink
Explains that in near-vacuum almost nothing slows the satellite down
Preserves the nuance that low orbits do slowly decay because of thin atmospheric drag
common_misconceptions: There is no gravity in orbit
Satellites need constant engine thrust to keep moving

critical_facts.fact: Gravity in low Earth orbit is still roughly 90% of its strength at the surface
At orbital speed, the satellite's path curves at the same rate as the Earth's surface curves away
Satellites in low orbit experience slight atmospheric drag and their orbits decay over time unless boosted

reasoning_gaps: Claiming orbits last forever (drops the drag caveat)
Re-explaining orbits from scratch

cases.question: What does 'like a thermostat' actually mean here? What does my body do when I get too hot?
cases.context: Earlier you explained: "Your body keeps its temperature near 37 C because the hypothalamus works like a thermostat."
expected_properties: Unpacks the analogy into the negative-feedback loop: sensing, comparison to a set point, and correction
Names the cooling responses (sweating, widening skin blood vessels) and why they shed heat
States where the thermostat analogy breaks, e.g. the set point can shift during fever
common_misconceptions: The hypothalamus directly heats or cools the body
Sweat cools by being cold rather than by evaporating

critical_facts.fact: Temperature regulation is a negative-feedback loop centred on the hypothalamus
Sweating cools the body mainly through evaporation
Vasodilation of skin blood vessels increases heat loss from the skin
During fever the body's temperature set point is raised

reasoning_gaps: Replacing one analogy with another without the mechanism
Listing responses without the feedback loop

cases.question: In PostgreSQL, why can a long-running transaction cause table bloat even if it only reads?
cases.audience: Experienced backend engineer familiar with PostgreSQL and MVCC terminology
expected_properties: Answers directly at expert level
Explains that VACUUM cannot remove dead row versions still visible to the oldest active snapshot
Does not introduce MVCC from scratch
Optionally gives monitoring or mitigation pointers
common_misconceptions: Read-only transactions cannot affect cleanup
VACUUM FULL is the routine fix

critical_facts.fact: Updates and deletes leave dead tuples under MVCC
VACUUM cannot remove tuples that may still be visible to the oldest running snapshot (the xmin horizon)
A long-running transaction, even a read-only one, can hold back that horizon, so dead tuples accumulate

reasoning_gaps: Tutorial-level MVCC introduction for an expert
Not naming the snapshot or horizon link

cases.question: On a simple quadratic loss, why does gradient descent diverge when the learning rate is too large?
expected_properties: Writes the update for f(x) = (a/2)x^2 and derives x_{k+1} = (1 - eta*a) x_k
States the divergence condition |1 - eta*a| > 1, i.e. eta > 2/a
Optionally notes oscillation for 1/a < eta < 2/a and the link to the largest curvature in higher dimensions
common_misconceptions: Any learning rate above 1 diverges
Divergence is caused by numerical precision

critical_facts.fact: For f(x) = (a/2)x^2, gradient descent gives x_{k+1} = (1 - eta*a) x_k
Iterates diverge when |1 - eta*a| > 1, i.e. eta > 2/a (for a > 0)
In higher dimensions the limit is set by the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian

reasoning_gaps: Intuition only, without the one-line derivation the audience expects
Explaining what gradient descent is

cases.question: Why does Cas9 need a PAM sequence next to its target site?
expected_properties: Explains that Cas9 first recognizes the PAM, then unwinds adjacent DNA to test guide complementarity
Explains the evolutionary role: distinguishing invading DNA from the bacterium's own CRISPR array
Does not explain what CRISPR or a guide RNA is
common_misconceptions: The PAM is part of the guide RNA
The PAM is only a lab convenience with no biological role

critical_facts.fact: SpCas9 recognizes the PAM 5'-NGG-3' adjacent to the target on the non-target strand
PAM binding triggers local unwinding so the guide RNA can interrogate the adjacent sequence
Requiring a PAM prevents Cas9 from cutting the bacterium's own CRISPR array, where spacers lack an adjacent PAM

reasoning_gaps: Introductory CRISPR background for an expert
Only the mechanistic or only the evolutionary reason

cases.question: What's the boiling point of water at sea level in Fahrenheit?
expected_properties: Answers 212 F in the first sentence
Adds at most one short clause of context

critical_facts.fact: Water boils at 212 F (100 C) at standard sea-level pressure

cases.question: Who wrote 'On the Origin of Species'?
expected_properties: Answers Charles Darwin directly
Does not add an unrequested explanation of evolution

critical_facts.fact: Charles Darwin wrote On the Origin of Species, published in 1859

cases.question: In one or two sentences: why do we have leap years?
expected_properties: Respects the one-to-two-sentence limit
Gives the cause: the year is about a quarter-day longer than 365 days, so the calendar would drift against the seasons
common_misconceptions: Every fourth year is always a leap year without exception

critical_facts.fact: The solar (tropical) year is about 365.24 days
Without the extra day the calendar would drift relative to the seasons

reasoning_gaps: Exceeding the requested length

cases.question: Translate into French: "The meeting has been moved to Thursday afternoon."
expected_properties: Gives the translation
No grammar lesson or explanation

critical_facts.fact: A correct translation, e.g. "La réunion a été déplacée à jeudi après-midi."

cases.question: Rewrite this to sound more formal: "hey, can you send me the report asap?"
expected_properties: Gives one or a few formal rewrites
No explanation of register unless very brief

critical_facts.fact: The rewrite keeps the meaning: a polite request to send the report soon

cases.question: Write a Python function that returns the n-th Fibonacci number using a loop.
expected_properties: Provides working iterative code
At most a brief note (e.g. on indexing convention); no tutorial on recursion or Fibonacci

critical_facts.fact: The function returns correct values for small n under its stated indexing convention (e.g. fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, fib(10)=55)

cases.question: Hi! How's your day going?
expected_properties: A short, natural greeting reply

cases.question:
This should return the last n items of a list, but it returns one too many. Fix it and briefly tell me what was wrong.

```python
def last_n(items, n):
    return items[len(items) - n - 1:]
```
expected_properties: Provides the fixed code first
Explains in one or two sentences that the start index should be len(items) - n, because slices start at the given index and include it
Optionally notes the n = 0 edge case of items[-n:]
common_misconceptions: Python slices exclude the start index

critical_facts.fact: items[len(items) - n:] returns the last n items
The original start index is one position too early, so it includes one extra item

reasoning_gaps: A long tutorial on slicing
